query_text: How much of sexual orientation is innate? Can being gay or straight be societally influenced?

annotations.title: No ‘gay gene’: Massive study homes in on genetic basis of human sexuality
Massive Study Finds No Single Genetic Cause of Same-Sex Sexual Behavior | Scientific American

content.text:
**Short answer:** sexual orientation appears to be **partly innate/biological, but not genetically predetermined**, and there is **little good evidence that society can make someone gay or straight** in the sense of changing their underlying pattern of attraction.

A useful way to separate it:

1. **Underlying attraction/orientation** — who someone is persistently attracted to.
2. **Identity** — whether they call themselves gay, straight, bi, queer, etc.
3. **Behavior** — who they date or have sex with.
4. **Expression/openness** — whether they disclose it or act on it.

Society can strongly influence **identity, behavior, and openness**. For example, in a very anti-gay society, fewer people may openly identify as gay or have same-sex relationships. In a more accepting society, more people may come out, experiment, or use labels like bisexual or queer. That does **not necessarily mean society created the underlying orientation**.

On innateness: research points to a **complex mix** of influences — genetics, prenatal development, hormones, possibly immune effects, and other non-social developmental factors. Large genetic studies have found that there is **no single “gay gene,”** but many genetic variants appear to make small contributions; one major 2019 genome-wide study found five associated genetic loci and emphasized that sexuality is highly complex and not predictable from DNA. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-019-02585-6?utm_source=openai))

The often-cited estimate from that 2019 work is that common genetic variation accounted for roughly **8–25% of variation in same-sex sexual behavior** in the studied populations, but this is **not the same as saying “orientation is 8–25% genetic”** for an individual. It was about behavior, not the full lived experience of orientation, and population-level variance estimates do not translate neatly to one person. ([scientificamerican.com](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/massive-study-finds-no-single-genetic-cause-of-same-sex-sexual-behavior/?utm_source=openai))

So “how much is innate?” The honest scientific answer is: **we do not have a precise percentage**. It is clearly **not 100% genetic**, but it is also not well explained as a voluntary choice or simple product of upbringing. Twin, family, genetic, and developmental research all suggest biological contributions, while leaving substantial room for non-genetic developmental factors.

Can society influence whether someone is gay or straight? **Probably not in the strong sense of changing their core orientation.** Social conditions can influence whether people recognize, label, suppress, disclose, or act on their attractions. They may also affect reported rates of LGBTQ identity because people feel safer saying so. But attempts to deliberately change orientation — often called “conversion therapy” or sexual orientation change efforts — have not been shown to reliably work and are considered potentially harmful by major mental-health organizations. The Royal College of Psychiatrists, for example, has stated that sexual orientation is not a choice and that attempts to change it lack evidence and can be harmful. ([rcpsych.ac.uk](https://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/docs/default-source/members/sigs/rainbow/resources/rainbow-sig-rcpsych-response-human-sexuality.pdf?sfvrsn=5a9b8eb0_4&utm_source=openai))

A balanced summary would be:

- **Genes matter, but there is no deterministic gay/straight gene.**
- **Prenatal and early developmental biology likely matter.**
- **Family upbringing, media exposure, or peer influence do not appear to “make” someone gay or straight.**
- **Culture strongly affects identity, disclosure, relationships, and reported prevalence.**
- **Some people experience fluidity, especially in identity or behavior, but that is not the same as society simply choosing or reprogramming orientation.**

So the best answer is: sexual orientation is **partly innate and biologically influenced**, **not a simple choice**, and **society mainly shapes how sexuality is expressed and understood rather than creating gayness or straightness from scratch**.
